newsitem.title: USA: Agency protects coho salmon in central California.
newsitem.headline: Agency protects coho salmon in central California.

text.p: The National Marine Fisheries Service said Friday it was protecting the dwindling central California coho salmon by listing the fish as a threatened species under the Endangered Species Act.

The service said it was deferring by six months a decision on whether to list two other coho salmon populations found in northern California and Oregon because of substantial scientific disagreement about their numbers and potential threats to their existence.
Environmentalists, farmers and California Gov. Pete Wilson all denounced the decisions, for different reasons.

Fisheries Service spokesman Brian Gorman said it was clear the central California coho salmon were in "dire straits". Their numbers had fallen from 100,000 in the 1940s to about 6,000 adults that were now returning each year to spawning streams. "That's enough to make anybody sit up and take notice," he said.

Fisheries service scientists said the coho's decline in California was caused by habitat degradation from logging, farming, flood control, mining, urbanization and hatchery practices as well as drought and poor ocean conditions.

Hilda Diaz-Soltero, Fisheries Service Southwest regional administrator, said federal agencies would work closely with government officials, private landowners, fishermen and environmental organizations on conservation measures to restore the coho salmon in the region.

Environmental groups petitioned the Fisheries Service several years ago to protect the coho -- also known as the silver salmon -- and the Fisheries Service was under federal court order to make a decision by Friday.

Once a species is listed under the Endangered Species Act, industrial activity, development and water usage that could harm its habitat are closely scrutinized by the authorities. There are already severe restrictions on salmon fishing off the U.S. Pacific coast.
The listing decision was seen as highly sensitive in an election year. Wilson, a Republican, and Oregon Gov. John Kitzhaber, a Democrat, had both asked the Fisheries Service to delay a decision.
Some environmentalists accused the agency of deferring to timber industry politics by putting off a decision on the northern California and Oregon coho salmon.

"By allowing timber companies to continue logging at unsustainable rates and destroying coho salmon habitat, the National Marine Fisheries Service is choosing to let this majestic species go extinct," Sierra Club official Elyssa Rosen said in a statement.

Wilson condemned the central California listing, saying it placed "logging, mining, ranching and other agricultural activities over large parts of the state at serious risk." He said the listing put timber land worth $4.6 billion off-limits to harvesting.

California Farm Bureau Federation President Bob Vice said the Fisheries Service had ignored scientific data that dispute claims the salmon are declining. "This is a flawed and premature listing which will severely handcuff important agricultural industries like timber and ranching...," he said.

Luke Popovich, spokesman for the American Forest and Paper Association, representing timber and paper companies, praised the Fisheries Service for postponing a decision in northern California and Oregon. "It would be silly to take precipitous action that could harm us and possibly the fish," he said.
